title: Chronic Liver Disease
subject: Medicine
summary: Chronic liver disease (CLD) is progressive hepatic injury leading to fibrosis and cirrhosis. In low‑resource African settings, viral hepatitis, alcohol, schistosomiasis and sickle‑cell disease dominate. Diagnosis relies on history, exam and limited investigations.

sections.p: CLD describes persistent hepatic injury (>6 months) with fibrosis, architectural distortion and functional impairment. Diagnosis requires a compatible history, physical signs and at least one objective test (ultrasound, serum markers or biopsy).
b: Fibrosis on imaging or biopsy confirms chronicity
ALT/AST elevation >6 months suggests ongoing injury
Absence of acute liver failure features

t.b: Does the liver show coarse echotexture, nodularity or splenomegaly? → Positive suggests fibrosis/cirrhosis; negative does not exclude early disease.
Is AST > ALT (ratio >2)? → Suggests alcoholic injury; ratio ≤1 points to viral or metabolic causes.
Is HBsAg or anti‑HCV positive? → Confirms viral etiology; if unavailable, rely on risk history.

sections.p: Cirrhosis is staged by compensated vs decompensated and by Child‑Pugh score (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy). MELD is used for transplant priority when labs are available.
b: Compensated: no ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleed
Decompensated: any of the above complications

t.b: Is bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL? → Indicates poorer synthetic function; raises Child‑Pugh score.
Is INR ≥1.7? → Reflects coagulation deficit; contributes to Child‑Pugh.
Is there clinically detectable ascites? → Moves patient to decompensated stage.

sections.p: In East Africa the commonest drivers are viral hepatitis B, alcohol misuse, schistosomiasis and sickle‑cell hepatopathy; HIV co‑infection and TB drug hepatotoxicity are also frequent.
b: Hepatitis B infection – endemic, often acquired perinatally
Chronic alcohol use – >40 g/day for men, >20 g/day for women
Schistosoma mansoni hepatic fibrosis – portal hypertension pattern
Sickle‑cell disease – repeated vaso‑occlusive hepatic injury
Hepatitis C – less common but important in transfusion‑exposed patients
Non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease – rising with urbanisation

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic early; later they develop fatigue, anorexia, right‑upper‑quadrant discomfort, jaundice, spider naevi, palmar erythema, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy.
b: Early: vague fatigue, mild RUQ discomfort
Compensated cirrhosis: splenomegaly, mild thrombocytopenia
Decompensated: ascites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, use bedside alternatives.

t.b: Is platelet count <150 000? → Thrombocytopenia suggests portal hypertension.
Is albumin <3.5 g/dL? → Low synthetic function; part of Child‑Pugh.
Are liver surface nodular and spleen enlarged? → Supports cirrhosis; if unavailable, rely on clinical stigmata.
Are esophageal varices present? → Guides prophylaxis; if unavailable, start non‑selective beta‑blocker in high‑risk patients.
Is creatinine rising rapidly in advanced CLD? → Raises suspicion for hepatorenal syndrome.

sections.p: Complications signal decompensation and high short‑term mortality; they demand urgent action.
b: New ascites or rapid increase in volume
Upper GI bleed (hematemesis/melena)
Altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy)
Jaundice with bilirubin >5 mg/dL
Renal dysfunction (creatinine >1.5 mg/dL) – possible hepatorenal syndrome

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, prevent decompensation, and manage complications. Use drugs that are affordable and safe in low‑resource settings.
b: Antiviral therapy for HBV (tenofovir) – suppresses viral replication, slows fibrosis
Alcohol abstinence counseling; consider baclofen if withdrawal risk
Hydroxyurea for sickle‑cell hepatopathy – reduces vaso‑occlusion
Non‑selective beta‑blocker (propranolol) for variceal bleed prophylaxis – lowers portal pressure
Lactulose for encephalopathy – acidifies colon, traps ammonia
Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic drugs – risk of renal failure

sections.p: Regular monitoring of liver function, viral load (if available), and screening for hepatocellular carcinoma (ultrasound every 6 months) are essential.
b: Clinic review every 3–6 months; repeat labs and ultrasound
Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B if not immune
Counsel on safe sex and clean needle use to prevent HBV/HCV
Screen for HCC with ultrasound; if unavailable, refer high‑risk patients

sections.p: Conditions that mimic CLD signs can mislead clinicians.
b: Heart failure – causes ascites and hepatomegaly but has peripheral edema and pulsus paradoxus
Non‑cirrhotic portal hypertension (e.g., schistosomiasis) – lacks synthetic dysfunction
Acute viral hepatitis – high transaminases >1000 U/L, no fibrosis

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite advanced disease.
b: AST/ALT may be only mildly elevated in cirrhosis; normal values do not exclude CLD
Serum bilirubin can be normal in compensated disease
Platelet count may be preserved early despite portal hypertension

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden massive abdominal distension (suspected ruptured variceal bleed)
Rapid rise in creatinine or oliguria

faq.q: Why is the AST/ALT ratio useful?
faq.a: A ratio >2 strongly suggests alcoholic liver injury, whereas a ratio ≤1 points to viral or metabolic causes.

faq.q: Can cirrhosis be present with normal liver enzymes?
faq.a: Yes; once fibrosis is established, transaminases often fall to near‑normal levels.
In any patient with hepatic encephalopathy to reduce ammonia absorption.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with chronic HBV presents with new ascites – what is your next immediate step? — Assess for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with diagnostic paracentesis and start empiric antibiotics if neutrophils ≥250.
How does schistosomiasis‑related portal hypertension differ from cirrhosis on investigation? — Ultrasound shows peri‑portal fibrosis without nodular liver surface; synthetic function often preserved.

Why is propranolol preferred over carvedilol for primary variceal prophylaxis in this setting? — Propranolol is widely available, inexpensive, and has a well‑studied safety profile; carvedilol may cause hypotension in patients with advanced disease.

A patient with known CLD develops confusion, asterixis and a serum ammonia of 85 µmol/L – what does this indicate and how do you manage? — Hepatic encephalopathy; start lactulose, correct precipitating factors, and consider rifaximin if available.
Explain the rationale for avoiding NSAIDs in a patient with decompensated cirrhosis. — NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis, precipitating hepatorenal syndrome and worsening ascites.

What are the Child‑Pugh criteria and how do they guide management? — Five variables (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) score 5‑15; class A can be observed, class C needs transplant evaluation and aggressive complication management.

In a resource‑limited hospital without MELD calculation, how would you prioritize patients for liver transplant? — Use Child‑Pugh C, refractory ascites, recurrent variceal bleed, or HRS as high‑priority indicators.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with jaundice and RUQ pain – how do you differentiate sickle‑cell hepatopathy from viral hepatitis? — Look for a history of vaso‑occlusive crises, normal viral serology, and rapid bilirubin rise with modest transaminase elevation.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic physical exam identify decompensation, aetiology and complications of chronic liver disease in low‑resource settings.
b: Ask about duration of symptoms, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss and jaundice.
Enquire about alcohol intake (grams/day), hepatitis B/C exposure, schistosomiasis exposure, sickle‑cell crises, and herbal medicines.
Screen for ascites (abdominal distension), oedema, variceal bleed (haematemesis/melena), encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis).
Ask about recent infections, NSAID use, pregnancy and HIV status.
Family history of liver disease and vaccination status for hepatitis B.

t.a: Inspection for spider naevi, palmar erythema, jaundice, ascites bulge
t.b: Detect chronic portal hypertension signs; presence suggests decompensation but cannot quantify portal pressure.

t.a: Palpation for liver span and tenderness
t.b: Enlarged, firm liver suggests active inflammation or HCC; cannot differentiate cause without imaging.
Suggests hepatic artery stenosis or arterio‑venous shunt; absent bruit does not exclude portal hypertension.
Positive indicates hepatic encephalopathy; does not grade severity beyond presence/absence.
Detects upper GI bleed; cannot locate source without endoscopy.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer a specific clinical question; when unavailable, use bedside surrogates or simple point‑of‑care tests.
b: Full blood count, liver function panel, coagulation profile, renal function, serum electrolytes.
Ultrasound with Doppler for liver texture, portal vein diameter, splenomegaly, ascites.
Serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) when ascitic fluid obtained.
HBV/HCV serology, HIV test, schistosomiasis serology where endemic.
Fibrosis scores (APRI, FIB‑4) if elastography unavailable.

t.b: Assess ongoing hepatocellular injury; ALT>AST suggests viral/NAFLD, AST/ALT>2 suggests alcoholic injury; values >5 × ULN raise suspicion of acute insult.
Elevated >2 mg/dL indicates impaired excretion; rising trend signals decompensation; direct >50 % suggests cholestasis.
Low <3.5 g/dL reflects synthetic failure; <2.8 g/dL defines Child‑Pugh C.
Prolonged >1.5 indicates reduced clotting factor synthesis; >2.0 mandates vitamin K trial and possible plasma.
Thrombocytopenia <150 ×10⁹/L suggests splenic sequestration; <100 ×10⁹/L increases bleeding risk.
Shows coarse echotexture, nodularity, portal vein >13 mm, splenomegaly; confirms chronicity when fibrosis seen.
Detects portal vein flow reversal or thrombosis; reversal indicates severe portal hypertension.
Calculate ascitic fluid albumin – serum albumin; ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension‑related ascites; <1.1 g/dL suggests peritoneal disease.
(AST/ULN ÷ platelet (10⁹/L)) × 100; >2 predicts cirrhosis; useful when elastography unavailable.
Identify chronic HBV infection; HBsAg positive >6 months confirms chronicity; high DNA guides antiviral need.
Positive antibody with detectable RNA confirms chronic HCV; guides treatment referral.
Positive indicates schistosomiasis; helps differentiate presinusoidal hypertension.

sections.p: Combine clinical, laboratory and imaging data to classify chronic liver disease and guide management decisions.
b: Diagnosis of CLD requires >6 months of liver injury plus evidence of fibrosis on imaging or biopsy.
Compensated cirrhosis: no ascites, encephalopathy or variceal bleed; decompensated: any of these complications present.
Child‑Pugh classification: assign points (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy); A = 5‑6, B = 7‑9, C = 10‑15.
MELD‑Na (if calculable): 3.78 × ln[bilirubin] + 11.2 × ln[INR] + 9.57 × ln[creatinine] + 6.43 × (1 if Na < 135 mEq/L); higher scores prioritize transplant.
APRI >2 or FIB‑4 >3.25 supports cirrhosis when elastography unavailable.
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL confirms portal‑hypertension ascites; guides diuretic therapy.
Presence of portal vein diameter >13 mm, splenomegaly and collateral veins on US defines clinically significant portal hypertension.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic chronic liver disease must be considered, especially in low‑resource settings where investigations are limited.
b: Congestive heart failure with hepatic congestion – presents with hepatomegaly, ascites, jaundice; differentiate by elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly on chest X‑ray.
Budd‑Chiari syndrome – painful hepatomegaly, ascites, rapid bilirubin rise; Doppler US shows hepatic vein thrombosis; absent in typical CLD.
Non‑cirrhotic portal hypertension (e.g., schistosomiasis) – splenomegaly, varices but preserved liver synthetic function; normal albumin and INR differentiate.
Hemochromatosis – bronze skin, diabetes, high ferritin; MRI or transferrin saturation >45 % distinguishes from CLD.

t.b: Key points: raised JVP, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly; bedside ultrasound of IVC collapsibility helps; liver enzymes modestly raised, not fibrotic pattern.
Key points: acute RUQ pain, tender hepatomegaly, ascites; Doppler US shows absent hepatic vein flow; labs show rapid INR rise, not chronic fibrosis.
Key points: history of freshwater exposure, eosinophilia, peri‑portal fibrosis on US; normal synthetic labs; stool ova confirms.
Key points: skin hyperpigmentation, diabetes, high ferritin/transferrin saturation; liver size may be enlarged but synthetic function often preserved early.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides acute stabilisation, treatment of the underlying aetiology, complication control and timely referral.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give O₂ if SpO₂ < 94 % and correct hypovolaemia with albumin 20 % if hypotensive.
2. Identify and treat the aetiology: start tenofovir/entecavir for HBV, advise alcohol abstinence, give praziquantel for schistosomiasis, manage NAFLD with weight loss.
3. Prevent first decompensation: start non‑selective β‑blocker (propranolol) if varices present, give diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide) for ascites, avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic drugs.
4. Monitor daily: weight, urine output, electrolytes, renal function, encephalopathy grade, and INR; adjust diuretics to achieve ≤ 0.5 kg loss/day.
5. Escalate when: refractory ascites, HE grade ≥ II, variceal bleed, MELD ≥ 15, or renal failure (creatinine > 2 mg/dL); arrange transfer for TIPS or transplant evaluation.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key medicines have predictable adverse profiles; recognising them avoids iatrogenic harm.
b: Propranolol – may cause bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue; if HR < 55 bpm or SBP < 90 mmHg, reduce dose or switch to carvedilol.
Spironolactone – risk of hyperkalaemia and gynecomastia; monitor K⁺ and switch to eplerenone if severe gynaecomastia.
Furosemide – can cause ototoxicity and volume depletion; check hearing if high doses, ensure adequate albumin replacement.
Tenofovir – renal tubular dysfunction; check serum creatinine and phosphate every 3 months, switch to entecavir if renal decline.
Ceftriaxone for SBP – may precipitate biliary sludge; limit to 5 days and monitor liver enzymes.

sections.p: Recognise decompensating events promptly; each has a clear trigger for higher‑level care.
b: New or worsening ascites with SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL – start albumin 1 g/kg and diuretics; if refractory, consider TIPS.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis – neutrophils > 250 cells/µL; give cefotaxime/ceftriaxone plus albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 then 1 g/kg day 3.
Variceal bleed – immediate IV octreotide, antibiotics (ceftriaxone), urgent endoscopy; if uncontrolled, arrange balloon tamponade and transfer.
Hepatic encephalopathy grade ≥ II – lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools, add rifaximin if refractory; ICU if coma.
Renal dysfunction (HRS‑A) – stop nephrotoxics, give albumin 1 g/kg then vasoconstrictor (terlipressin if available); early transplant referral.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, test interpretation and therapy choices.
b: HIV – lower CD4 may mask typical signs; avoid protease inhibitors that raise bilirubin; prioritize HBV-active ART.
TB – rifampicin induces CYP enzymes, reducing levels of β‑blockers and antivirals; monitor drug levels if possible.
Malnutrition – low albumin worsens ascites; give high‑protein diet and consider oral supplements.
Pregnancy – avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., ribavirin); use beta‑blocker propranolol cautiously, monitor fetal growth.
Diabetes – metformin contraindicated in decompensation; use insulin sliding scale; watch for hypoglycaemia with reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis.
Herbal remedies (e.g., kava, traditional concoctions) – may contain hepatotoxins; obtain a thorough medication history.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and therapy to age, pregnancy status and resource constraints.
b: Children – use weight‑based dosing of antivirals; screen for congenital HBV; avoid adult‑dose diuretics; monitor growth.
Pregnant women – prioritize safe antivirals (tenofovir), avoid teratogenic agents, manage ascites with low‑dose spironolactone only if benefits outweigh risks.
Elderly – start β‑blocker at low dose, watch for orthostatic hypotension; renal function often reduced, adjust diuretics accordingly.
People with HIV – choose HBV therapy that also suppresses HIV (tenofovir + lamivudine/FTC); coordinate with HIV team.

Low‑resource settings – when ultrasound unavailable, use bedside fluid wave and shifting dullness for ascites; use clinical scoring (Child‑Pugh) instead of MELD; procure generic propranolol and spironolactone.

facts: Chronic liver disease is defined by hepatic injury >6 months with fibrosis on imaging or biopsy.
Compensated cirrhosis: no ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleed; decompensated: any of these complications.
Child‑Pugh score: A (5‑6), B (7‑9), C (10‑15) using bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy.
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension‑related ascites; SAAG <1.1 g/dL suggests non‑portal causes.
AST/ALT ratio >1 with thrombocytopenia often points to alcoholic liver disease.
Upper GI variceal bleed prophylaxis: non‑selective β‑blocker (propranolol) target HR 55‑60 bpm.
MELD‑Na calculation not required for basic triage; prioritize patients with MELD ≥15 or Child‑Pugh C.
Hepatitis B endemic in East Africa; perinatal transmission accounts for >50% of chronic infections.

mnemonics.t: C = encephalopathy, H = ascites, I = INR, L = bilirubin, D = albumin – each scored 1‑3 for Child‑Pugh.
Serum‑Ascites Albumin Gradient; high (≥1.1) = portal hypertension, low (<1.1) = other causes.

vivas.q: Define chronic liver disease and how chronicity is confirmed.
vivas.a: Persistent hepatic injury >6 months; confirmed by fibrosis on imaging (ultrasound elastography) or liver biopsy.

vivas.q: What bedside examination steps confirm ascites and what does each test show?
vivas.a: Inspection for distended abdomen, percussion for flank dullness, shifting dullness (fluid moves to dependent side), fluid thrill (tapping midline). Positive tests indicate free fluid; they cannot quantify volume.

vivas.q: Interpret a SAAG of 1.3 g/dL with ascitic fluid total protein 0.8 g/dL.
vivas.a: High SAAG (>1.1) indicates portal hypertension; low protein (<1.0) suggests sinusoidal cause such as cirrhosis.

vivas.q: Why are NSAIDs avoided in decompensated cirrhosis?
vivas.a: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis, precipitating renal failure in patients with already compromised renal perfusion from portal hypertension.

vivas.q: How does schistosomiasis‑related portal hypertension differ from cirrhosis on imaging?
vivas.a: Schistosomiasis shows peri‑portal fibrosis with preserved hepatic architecture; cirrhosis shows nodular surface and diffuse parenchymal nodularity.

vivas.q: A patient with CLD develops new ascites and a sudden INR rise while bilirubin is stable. Which finding most suggests acute decompensation?
vivas.a: The abrupt increase in INR reflects loss of synthetic function and is the key marker of acute decompensation.

vivas.q: What are the primary collagen‑secreting cells in hepatic fibrosis?
vivas.a: Activated hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) transform into myofibroblasts and produce type I and III collagen.

vivas.q: Explain why propranolol is preferred over carvedilol for primary variceal prophylaxis in low‑resource settings.
vivas.a: Propranolol is inexpensive, widely available, and its β‑blockade alone reduces portal pressure; carvedilol adds α‑blockade but has higher hypotension risk and limited supply.

vivas.q: A patient with CLD is given diazepam. What pharmacokinetic change is expected with repeated dosing?
vivas.a: Reduced hepatic metabolism leads to drug accumulation and prolonged half‑life, increasing sedation risk.

vivas.q: Describe the typical histological triad of alcoholic hepatitis.
vivas.a: Ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes, Mallory‑Denk bodies, and neutrophilic lobular infiltrates.

vivas.q: What bedside sign differentiates hepatic encephalopathy from metabolic delirium?
vivas.a: Asterixis (flapping tremor) on outstretched hands is characteristic of hepatic encephalopathy.

vivas.q: When should a patient with compensated cirrhosis be referred for transplant evaluation?
vivas.a: When Child‑Pugh C or recurrent decompensation (ascites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy) occurs despite optimal medical therapy.

vivas.q: How does HIV co‑infection modify the natural history of chronic hepatitis B?
vivas.a: HIV accelerates HBV replication, increases risk of cirrhosis and HCC, and may blunt response to antiviral therapy.

vivas.q: What is the first step in managing a new‑onset variceal bleed in a resource‑limited hospital?
vivas.a: Stabilize haemodynamics, give IV octreotide (if available) or terlipressin, and start prophylactic antibiotics; arrange urgent endoscopy.

vivas.q: Why is the AST/ALT ratio >2 suggestive of alcoholic liver disease?
vivas.a: Alcohol preferentially damages mitochondria, raising AST (mitochondrial) more than ALT (cytosolic), giving a ratio >2.

vivas.q: What is the expected platelet count mechanism in portal hypertension?
vivas.a: Splenic sequestration due to hypersplenism lowers platelet count, independent of bone‑marrow production.

vivas.q: A patient with CLD presents with a painful subareolar breast lump. What is the likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Galactocele or fibrocystic change secondary to estrogen excess; histology shows dense fibrous stroma and ductal hyperplasia.

vivas.q: What is the recommended surveillance interval for hepatocellular carcinoma in HBV‑related cirrhosis?
vivas.a: Ultrasound every 6 months, with AFP optional, regardless of age in endemic regions.

mcqs.q: A 48‑year‑old man with known HBV cirrhosis presents with new abdominal distension. Which laboratory result most strongly supports portal‑hypertensive ascites?
mcqs.e: SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension‑related ascites.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the Child‑Pugh score?
mcqs.e: Serum sodium is used in MELD‑Na, not Child‑Pugh.

mcqs.q: A patient with alcoholic cirrhosis has AST 210 U/L, ALT 80 U/L. Which interpretation is correct?
o: AST/ALT ratio >2 suggests alcoholic liver disease
mcqs.e: Alcoholic injury raises AST disproportionately, giving ratio >2.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource setting without elastography, which bedside test helps estimate fibrosis stage?
mcqs.e: Thrombocytopenia correlates with portal hypertension and advanced fibrosis.

mcqs.q: Which medication should be avoided in a patient with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites?
mcqs.e: NSAIDs impair renal perfusion and precipitate renal failure.

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with CLD develops confusion, asterixis, and ammonia 85 µmol/L. What is the next immediate management step?
mcqs.e: Lactulose is first‑line to reduce ammonia and improve encephalopathy.

mcqs.q: Which finding best differentiates schistosomal portal hypertension from cirrhosis on ultrasound?
mcqs.e: Schistosomiasis shows peri‑portal fibrosis without nodular regeneration.

mcqs.q: A patient with chronic HBV is started on tenofovir. Which monitoring parameter is essential?
mcqs.e: ALT tracks viral activity and drug efficacy.

cases.v: A 42‑year‑old male farmer with known chronic hepatitis B presents with increasing abdominal girth over 2 weeks, mild peripheral edema, and mild jaundice. Examination: shifting dullness positive, spleen palpable 3 cm, no asterixis.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of his new ascites?
qs.a: Portal hypertension secondary to progression of cirrhosis.

qs.q: Which bedside test confirms the presence of ascites and how is it performed?
qs.a: Shifting dullness: percuss flank while patient lies supine, then turn to side; fluid shifts to dependent side, making that area dull.

qs.q: What immediate management step should be taken?
qs.a: Control fluid accumulation with low‑sodium diet and start diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide) while arranging ultrasound to assess liver and rule out infection.

cases.v: A 58‑year‑old woman with alcohol‑related cirrhosis (Child‑Pugh B) presents with hematemesis. She is hypotensive (BP 90/60), pulse 110, and has a flapping tremor. No prior endoscopy.

qs.q: What is the first emergency intervention?
qs.a: Resuscitate with IV crystalloids, give blood transfusion to maintain Hb >8 g/dL, and start IV octreotide (or terlipressin).

qs.q: Which drug is recommended for primary variceal prophylaxis after stabilisation?
qs.a: Propranolol, titrated to achieve heart rate 55‑60 bpm.

qs.q: Why should antibiotics be given even before endoscopy?
qs.a: Pre‑emptive antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) reduce risk of bacterial infection and re‑bleeding in cirrhotic variceal hemorrhage.

mistakes: Confusing a low SAAG (<1.1) with portal hypertension; low SAAG indicates non‑portal causes.
Using AST/ALT ratio >1 as sole proof of alcoholic disease without considering other causes.
Prescribing NSAIDs in decompensated cirrhosis, leading to renal failure.
Failing to adjust diuretic doses for electrolyte monitoring, causing hyponatremia.
Assuming normal INR rules out synthetic failure; INR can be normal early in decompensation.
Neglecting to give prophylactic antibiotics before variceal bleed endoscopy.
Relying on ultrasound alone for fibrosis staging when elastography is unavailable; combine platelet count and clinical signs.
Overlooking HIV co‑infection, which accelerates HBV progression and alters antiviral choice.
